newsitem.title: USA: EMU seen ultimately pressuring dollar - study.
newsitem.headline: EMU seen ultimately pressuring dollar - study.

text.p: The transition to a single European currency could fuel a temporary dollar rally but may ultimately weaken the U.S. unit, according to Randall Henning, visiting fellow at the Institute for International Economics.

Europe's proposed economic and monetary union (EMU) will reduce demand for dollars on international transactions and in central bank vaults as the new euro slowly emerges as a viable alternative currency, Henning wrote in a recent analysis.
"The new European currency will probably grow into this role over time. There will be no precipitous displacement of the dollar by the euro at the outset of EMU," Henning said.

The dollar could temporarily rise amid investor concerns over the new European Central Bank's commitment to anti-inflationary monetary policy, but reverse course as the ECB establishes it credibility, according to Henning.
"These movements could produce a good deal of exchange rate instability between the dollar and European currencies, and then the euro, during the transition, Henning wrote.

Eliminating several European currencies would relieve governments of the task of stabilizing them. That would free up huge hoards of cash earmarked for this purpose that could now be spent or swapped into euros.
Some analysts estimate the size of this pool of redundant reserves, of which dollars comprise by far the largest share, at over $100 billion.
Cash-strapped European governments will likely view this money as a windfall, to be used to pay down debt or boost domestic spending, Henning wrote.

"Excess reserves appear to be sufficiently large to raise serious questions about how they will be managed," said Henning. "Some of these uses raise potential problems, including downward pressure on the dollar exchange rate."

The Institute of International Economics is headed by Fred Bergsten, a tireless advocate of a weaker dollar and suspected by some of exerting influence over some Clinton Administration economic officials.
Henning's report repeated that warning of an overvalued dollar, citing the large U.S. current account deficit and shrinking budget shortfalls.
Henning criticized the policy of Group of Seven industrialized nations that helped push the dollar to multiyear highs early this year.

"If (IIE's) analysis is correct, the G7 has sown the seeds of a major exchange rate correction. Depending on when it occurs, the correction could well threaten the achievement of monetary union itself," wrote Henning.

The dollar currently stands near 1.71 marks, having rallied to nearly 1.74 in late April. The greenback is up 27 percent from its post-World War II low at 1.3438 marks in March 1995 and has risen 11 percent in 1997.
